articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before".
Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said traffic had partially resumed on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - after they had been closed following Russian strikes overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The Kremlin said Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: U.S. military takes custody of Army officer accused of spying for Russia after U.K. arrest
articles.title_zh: U.S. military takes custody of Army officer accused of spying for Russia after U.K. arrest
articles.content_orig:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

articles.title_orig: ‘Do not build’: UK sanctions 8 Israeli construction companies for building West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: ‘Do not build’: UK sanctions 8 Israeli construction companies for building West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank .
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers .
Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
after newsletter promotion
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

articles.title_orig: Dow drops more than 800 points, S&P 500 posts lowest close since July
articles.title_zh: Dow drops more than 800 points, S&P 500 posts lowest close since July
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities tumbled on Tuesday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite hitting its lowest level in roughly seven months, as traders sold off semiconductor names ahead of Nvidia's much-anticipated earnings report.
Reports of a National Security Agency network outage added to recent jitters about the stability of the country's technology infrastructure and helped weigh on the market, traders said.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848.75 points, or 1.64%, to end at 50,759.42. It dropped more than 1,000 points at its session low. The S&P 500 fell 1.03% to 7,340.53, for its lowest closing level since late July. The broad market index sank as low as 1.7% earlier in the session.
The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.74%. At one point during Tuesday's session, it sank by as much as roughly 2.1% to touch its lowest level since April.
Major averages fell to their lows of the day following the report from CNN that said a classified network used by the spy agency had gone down, citing six people familiar with the matter. CNN's sources said there was no evidence that it was a cyberattack.
The NSA later in the day put out a statement saying the agency "experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The agency added that "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational."
Traders said the report helped take equities lower, though the losses were contained. This outage is latest in a string of incidents that have left people on edge including the FAA ground stop over the weekend, Microsoft's Outlook outage last week and some recent issues with banking apps.
Nvidia shares ended the session 0.5% lower amid investors' handwringing ahead of the company's earnings report due after the closing bell. However, the stock got a short-lived boost earlier in the session after Jensen Huang said he would be open to returning as CEO if the company's board thought that was in the best interest of shareholders.
"Nvidia should report strong results and guidance, but [it] is unlikely to be able to give investors solid answers to the questions heavily weighing on the stock [regarding] leadership and investigations around export controls," Ross Mayfield, investment strategist at Baird, told CNBC. "Strong demand might stabilize things, but the next leg higher will need some clarification around the 2028 and beyond outlook."
Other tech players ended the day in negative territory but well off their session lows, with Micron Technology sliding 0.9%. Advanced Micro Devices slipped 0.2%, while Intel was down 0.5%.
Microsoft shares were down 2%.
Neocloud stock Iren shed more than 3%. Nebius lost 1%. Investor Steve Eisman told CNBC earlier in the day that these stocks were among the names with the most to lose if the Huang scandal causes Nvidia to pull back its financing of the AI ecosystem.
U.S. equities closed lower on Tuesday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 848.75 points, or 1.64%, lower at 50,759.42. It fell more than 1,000 points at its session low.
The S&P 500 shed 1.03% to end the session at 7,340.53, for its lowest closing level since late July. The broad market index sank as low as 1.73% earlier in the session.
The Nasdaq Composite was down 0.74% to 24,328.38 at the closing bell. At one point, it sank by as much as roughly 2.1% to hit its lowest level since April.
The VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose as much as 21% to an intraday high of 27.73, the highest since Nov. 6.
The VIX is now on track to rise for a fourth consecutive day for the first time since August 28.
Recent market volatility doesn't change UBS' conviction in the opportunity in artificial intelligence or its constructive view on diversified equities.
Investors weighing AI demand and the elevated capital expenditures from tech companies have sent stocks lower.
"Still, for the sell-off to indicate a lasting deterioration in the AI investment cycle, we would need to see weakening compute demand, slowing AI- related revenue growth, poor capacity utilization, or tighter financial conditions constraining spending by the largest technology platforms, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer for Americas, said in a note Tuesday.
Breadth of selling will also matter, and there is no evidence of that yet. Underlying demand for computing capacity also remains robust, he noted.
"We therefore continue to see potential for gains in broad equity markets over the next six to 12 months, supported by resilient economic growth and corporate earnings," Hoffmann-Burchardi wrote. "Near-term volatility reinforces the importance of selectivity and disciplined portfolio construction rather than a broadly defensive stance."
A CNN report Tuesday that a classified network used by the National Security Agency is down was just the latest to hit a stock market that's been battered lately by negative headlines. These include the FAA ground stop over the weekend, as well as Microsoft's Outlook outage last week.
"Any one of the stories that have have broken over the course of the last week or so would be enough to cause the market jitters. But when you compound that by having multiple stories — whether it's today's NSA report or the FAA ground halt or Microsoft Outlook being down for two days or Chase Bank ATMs not working — aggregate all of those, and it's easy for the human mind to get to a place where there must be something larger at play here," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth. "What's causing the market to have the kind of drawdowns that it's having today, it's just that aggregate of the compounding of bizarre stories that just have become too much of a headwind, at least in the near term," he added.
Investors may not be moved by Nvidia's upcoming earnings results, according to Megan Horneman, chief investment officer at Verdence Capital Advisors.
"I don't think there's going to be anything surprising from the earnings report," she told CNBC. "I don't know that we're even going to get much forward-looking information that people may be trying to get information on."
Horneman expects uncertainty to persist for the technology sector as investors assess what the trade could look like after "parts of Nvidia start to unwind."
"We're just stuck in this, I think, panic type of stage right now, and I don't know how far it will go," she said.
Another strong round of economic data, particularly on the consumer side, has led Goldman Sachs to take up its growth forecast.
The firm now sees  fourth quarter gross domestic product accelerating by a 2.4% annualized pace, up 0.6 percentage point from its prior outlook. Moreover, Goldman raised its backward-looking expectation for the third quarter, now looking for 3.8% growth from the period, which would be 0.4 percentage point higher than the advance estimate from the Commerce Department.
At the core of the more optimistic outlook is a retail sales report Tuesday that showed receipts up 0.2% in October — 0.6% when excluding autos and when focusing on the components that feed directly to GDP.
"The strength of today's report continues to reflect the resilience of the US consumer this year, as boosts from tax refunds and positive wealth effects from equity market gains have more than offset the drag from higher energy prices," Goldman chief economist Jan Hatzius said in a note.
Selling was broad across Wall Street midday Tuesday as declining stocks outnumbered advancers by nearly 3 to 1 on both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.
Declining volume accounted for roughly 69% of total NYSE volume and 71% on the Nasdaq, according to FactSet data.
On the NYSE, 1,924 stocks declined while only 700 rose. For Nasdaq, decliners totaled 3,036, compared with 1,141 advancers.
New lows also outpaced new highs. The NYSE recorded 362 new lows against just 20 new highs, while the Nasdaq logged 679 new lows versus 38 new highs.

articles.title_orig: Following Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Gmail outage has hit. Marriott down too [Update]
articles.title_zh: Following Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Gmail outage has hit. Marriott down too [Update]
articles.content_orig:
Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard .
As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.
The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.
The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.
However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”
Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.
As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Russian military plane crashes, killing all 19 on board
articles.title_zh: Russian military plane crashes, killing all 19 on board
articles.content_orig:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

articles.title_orig: California bans Waymo autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an 'imminent hazard'
articles.title_zh: California bans Waymo autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an 'imminent hazard'
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks.
Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.
The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”
Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.
Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.
In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.
Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.
That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.
If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares closed marginally lower Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
The stock move Tuesday marked Nvidia's fourth straight daily decline.
In the statement, Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
US investigators conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang last summer, the US Commerce and Justice Departments said, as part of an investigation into whether the Singapore-based company had been diverting highly coveted US semiconductors.
The departments included that detail in a joint statement released late Monday, which laid out a timeline of their investigation into the cloud computing and data center provider. The Commerce Department launched an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations, the departments said.
The statement comes after days of mounting scrutiny of US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for being too slow in taking action against Megaspeed. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added to the pressure on Friday , accusing the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling the Nvidia customer a possible national security threat.
The departments said Commerce investigators requested records in May 2025 from Nvidia concerning “direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed,” and that Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list the following month.
Following that, agents from agents from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, “conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang,” the joint statement said.
Lies, spies and sex are just one part of the Nvidia story. The real stakes are much bigger
US government officials have identified Alice Huang as having had an affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and have raised concerns that she could be a potential Chinese intelligence asset. The US intelligence community has been working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
Megaspeed said in a statement Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and currently holds no role there. It also said that the company is “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence.”
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Monday’s statement offered few other details, but said that the Justice Department has since taken on the lead role in the criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
The statement follows similar details released last week by the Singaporean government, which also noted US authorities’ visit to Megaspeed last summer. It said the Bureau of Industry and Security conducted a check at Megaspeed, “with Huang present,” on June 24, 2025, which “was the first time Singapore came to know about the US’s interest in Megaspeed and Huang,” the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement .
That same day, Singaporean police also interviewed her as part of its ongoing investigations into Megaspeed, and her passport was impounded to secure her attendance for purposes of the ongoing investigations, since Alice Huang was not based in Singapore, the statement said.
Ultimately, the Singapore Police Force concluded there was “insufficient evidence” that Alice Huang had committed any offenses relating to the investigation, but she was barred from re-entering the country due to attempts to “downplay her role” at Megaspeed, the government said.
CNN’s Stephanie Yang contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.title_zh: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title_orig: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody
articles.title_zh: American soldier held in UK suspected of spying for Russia taken into US military custody
articles.content_orig:
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.
The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.
“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.
“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.
“Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”
The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.
He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.
US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.
He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.
As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.
Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.
“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.
“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution”.
He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.
“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The funding would go to new air traffic control centers and other improvements.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee sent a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration's Bryan Bedford on Tuesday demanding an explanation for Friday's nationwide ground stop and calling for briefings before there are additional changes to the air traffic control system.
It comes the same day the Department of Transportation has officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix a system Duffy and President Donald Trump say is broken . The budget breakdown includes more than $10 billion for the completion of a reliable digital architecture, more than $10 billion to overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, $10 billion to build five new air traffic control centers and another $10 billion to build and improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.
Duffy has said the $50 billion funding ask, which is in addition to the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress, is needed to fix the issues that led to the ground stop.
"This is an emergency," he told reporters Friday night. "I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."
In their letter, Democrats said that Friday's ground stop "disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions" about the FAA and its ability to ensure reliable operations.
"Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it," the 13 Democrats on the committee wrote in the letter.
The senators addressed Duffy's funding request -- noting that the increase from $30 billion to $50 billion following Friday's ground stop "is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12."
"DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote.
Ahead of a meeting with Duffy on Tuesday, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said the funding request needs to be detailed.
"If you want $30 billion or $50 billion, you better damn sure have a long list of initiatives and planning that went into it versus ‘give me a number and I'll figure out how to spend it.’”
GOP Sen. John Cornyn said when it comes to FAA funding, he would like to know "what they have, why they haven't spent it and why they need more."
The Democratic senators also raised questions about devices from Juniper -- the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop -- as well as L3 Harris, a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the FAA and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.
The ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday; FAA Administrator Bedford added that it was the result of faulty equipment.
Duffy told ABC's "This Week" Sunday that work was being done to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred. When the router in that area was turned on, "we saw that in Amarillo, Texas, a system we had replaced about three weeks earlier, that started to flood our system as well," Duffy explained.
In the letter, the senators requested a pause on the installation of additional Juniper devices -- the devices that are replacing routers in the copper-to-fiber transition -- until further testing demonstrates that they can be deployed safely.
The lawmakers say they expect a briefing on those improvements before installation continues.
"Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices' readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures," they said.
The FAA announced Tuesday afternoon that it was halting the installation of Juniper routers .
The senators requested technical briefings from the FAA, L3 Harris and Juniper by Monday. Those briefings should include an initial safety assessment and explanations about how the system lacked sufficient redundancy to immediately recover during Friday's ground stop, the senators wrote in the letter.
The outage, they write, has left them "concerned" about DOT's ability to oversee the new air traffic control system.
"Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote.
Asked for comment on the letter, a DOT spokesperson said "The Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so."
Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the ranking member of the Commerce Aviation, Space and Innovation subcommittee who is among the Democrats who signed the letter, has said Duffy is "unfit to serve" in his role if he is not able to answer questions about the ground stop.
"If the Secretary cannot take responsibility and provide answers, he is unfit to serve as the Secretary of Transportation," Duckworth said in a statement to Politico.
Trump has praised Duffy amid concern over the ground stop, saying on Monday that Duffy is "doing a great job."
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain, and US retaliation
articles.title_zh: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain, and US retaliation
articles.content_orig:
By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart
DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US and Iran exchanged fire on Tuesday, with the US striking an Iranian missile launch site after Iran said it targeted a US military radar system in Bahrain, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.
The latest back-and-forth between the US and Iran ‌was a reminder of difficulties ending nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and fueled US voter anger in November ‌elections that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party.
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to Iran's "aggression targeting ​US personnel and assets." Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier on Tuesday they targeted a US military radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy.
Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage.
Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.
They coincide with a visit to ‌Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he ⁠discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister.
Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before ⁠the war but is now partly blocked by Iran.
Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait.
Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS
The war has ground to a stalemate, with Trump saying he might ​hold ​off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the ​Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen.
Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously ‌the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations."
Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers ‌had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.
Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% ​at $92.76 a barrel, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41.
The war continues to spill ​over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington ​through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf ‌oil producers.
Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni ​Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, ​mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state.
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs.
Iran also fired on Bahrain on Sunday, saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what ​it said were hostile US actions.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi ‌said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes," which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the ​sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority."
These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," Mohebbi said.
(Additional reporting by Yomna Ehab and Elwely Elwelly, Writing by ​Nayera Abdallah, Aidan Lewis and Phil Stewart; Editing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Don Durfee and Rod Nickel)

articles.title_orig: NC approves Duke Energy rate hikes, new rules for data centers
articles.title_zh: NC approves Duke Energy rate hikes, new rules for data centers
articles.content_orig:
Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand.
For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job.
Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up.
“I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said.
About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect.
The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests.
Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills.
The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season.
According to projections released Tuesday by Duke Energy, a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month would see the following increases:
Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina):
Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region):
That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges.
Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans.
Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills.
The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled.
Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs.
Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth.
“We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.”
For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect.
Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding.
“I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said.
The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days.
For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts.
The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas.
Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission.
Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure.
Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. Without additional safeguards, other customers could be left paying for infrastructure if anticipated data center demand fails to materialize or companies leave prematurely.
New financial requirements for qualifying data center projects and expansions include:
The commission also established requirements for data centers to temporarily reduce electricity demand under certain circumstances to help maintain grid reliability.
Duke said Tuesday that regulators retained many of the company's existing data center requirements while adding financial protections intended to shield other customers from the costs and risks of serving new facilities.
Environmental advocates welcomed the new financial requirements while calling for additional measures to address the costs of generating electricity for data centers.
“This is a big step forward to ensuring that data centers pay their fair share of the costs of connecting to the grid,” said Will Scott, North Carolina policy director for the Environmental Defense Fund. “Now we need to take the next step and enable them to pay for their own new clean energy and batteries to avoid regular customers bearing the cost of unnecessary new gas plants.”
Duke indicated in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday that it is evaluating the data center provisions and will continue working with customers and other stakeholders on implementation.
Monday's rate decisions came alongside a separate ruling approving Duke's latest long-term energy plan, which extends the operation of some coal plants and calls for nearly 3,850 megawatts of new natural gas generation, alongside additional solar generation and battery storage.
The decisions come ahead of the planned merger of Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress into a single utility on Jan. 1, 2027.
Duke must now work with the Public Staff, the state agency representing utility customers, to finalize its revenue calculations before the new rates take effect.
For Brooks, the immediate concern is how to stretch her household budget even further. She is considering taking another part-time job, even if it means sacrificing time with her grandchildren.
“It's just that it's so high that you're struggling to pay because you need to keep your lights on,” Brooks said. “You gotta have your refrigerator so you can put your stuff in it. It's just heartbreaking.”

articles.content_orig:

Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
