articles.title_orig: Oregon sues OpenAI for $2 billion, says ChatGPT puts kids in harm’s way
articles.title_zh: Oregon sues OpenAI for $2 billion, says ChatGPT puts kids in harm’s way
articles.content_orig:
Chat GPT app icon is seen on a smartphone screen, Monday, Aug. 4, 2025, in Chicago. (AP Photo/Kiichiro Sato)
Oregon’s top law enforcement officials sued OpenAI on Tuesday over concerns that the artificial intelligence company and its chatbots are harming the state’s youth.
In its lawsuit, the Oregon Department of Justice accused OpenAI of violating the state’s consumer protection laws by misrepresenting its flagship product, ChatGPT, as safe for kids. The agency alleged the company has known the chatbot lacks guardrails to protect minors yet continues to market to them.
The AI bot has helped children plan suicides and commit acts of violence, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield told OPB. He said OpenAI is aware of the dangers its products can pose.
“OpenAI continues to look parents in the eyes and say this product is a safe product when it’s continuing to cause harm in our communities,” Rayfield said.
The lawsuit comes as the company, and the burgeoning AI industry, grapple with public fears that it is coaching users to self-harm and carry out attacks on others. Eight U.S. states sued OpenAI in October, each claiming the technology is dangerously influential on teens.
OpenAI allows users as young as 13 years old, so long as they have a parent or guardian’s consent. The state’s 53-page complaint states the company often fails to confirm that a parent signed off for an underage user.
The company also recently released a “ChatGPT for Teens” version that would link a parent’s account to their child’s. But Oregon Department of Justice officials wrote that the version’s purportedly stronger safeguards are easily bypassed. They said this version did not alert parents when a young user asked about risky topics including suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or mental health issues.
The complaint accused OpenAI of misrepresenting its products in violation of Oregon’s Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The complaint said the company’s violations were “willful” and “constituted unfair, unjust, shocking, and unconscionable outcome.”
The state agency’s complaint called on OpenAI to institute stronger safeguards and compensate Oregonians with at least $2.035 billion dollars in damages.
In past statements, the company has insisted that keeping communities safe is a “top priority.”
Following the lawsuits by multiple states, an OpenAI spokesperson issued a statement saying, “We’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as parental controls, break reminders, and age-appropriate model protections that exist today.”
Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI spokesperson, issued a nearly identical statement Tuesday after Oregon’s lawsuit. Pusateri wrote the company is committed to developing AI policies “that apply to the entire AI industry and not just one company.”
Rayfield said in an interview that there was no specific incident in Oregon that led his office to file suit. He said the suit arose from incidents across the country and his office’s concern that technology advancement is outpacing consumer protections.
“How do we responsibly use these technologies?” Rayfield said. “They can be incredibly amazing if their promises come through, but at the same time, what we’re seeing on the other side is devastation.”
Questions about teens’ use of AI and online platforms have been particularly prevalent in Oregon lately, in the wake of multiple high-profile incidents.
The teen who shot and killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend last month has been linked by multiple sources to online extremist groups, though investigators have not yet revealed whether those ties are significant to the shooting.
The Multnomah County District Attorney’s office similarly blamed online extremist groups for influencing a Benson High School student to release toxic chemicals at school in September.
Rayfield declined to say whether OpenAI’s products had any involvement in those incidents, citing the ongoing investigation.

articles.title_orig: Costco Shoppers Are Panic-Buying Due to Outages, Analysts Say
articles.title_zh: Costco Shoppers Are Panic-Buying Due to Outages, Analysts Say
articles.content_orig:
Costco shoppers are panic-buying bottled water, generators and batteries as apocalyptic social media posts gain traction online following a series of freak outages over the past few days.
Toward the end of October, Costco saw “increased buying on certain items including rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, batteries and similar items seemingly in response to a variety of concerns on social media,” Chief Financial Officer Gary Millerchip told Bloomberg.
As of Sunday, “21 of the 26 high-ticket generators the company offers online were sold out,” analysts at Mizuho Securities wrote in a note.
The analysts said the buying spree started in the final week of October and has continued through November, adding that they expect all the shopping will boost Costco’s sales.
Last week, a Microsoft Outlook and Teams outage left workers across the country unable to send emails or take work calls for days.
Then the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for just the second time since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks – canceling thousands of flights and leaving passengers stranded at airports.
Microsoft resolved the issue after roughly 24 hours and said it was caused by a server issue, not by a cyberattack or out-of-control AI.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also later revealed that the rare ground stop was caused by a botched contractor job or faulty router as workers were ripping out aging copper telecom wires for fiber optic lines.
But conspiracy theories had already taken off online. And new outages this week hitting JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines and Apple Pay were the perfect fuel for doomsdayers, who have spread theories about government plots, blackouts, cyberattacks and rogue AI bots.
As the social-media posts send anxious consumers rushing to stock up on necessities, retailers like Walmart and its warehouse brand Sam’s Club; Home Depot; Lowe’s; and even Tractor Supply could see similar sales lifts, according to analysts at Mizuho Securities.
The firm has hiked its price target for Costco shares from $1,100 to $1,150, partially due to the strength of the panic-buying. The stock traded roughly flat on Tuesday at $1,110.08 a share.
Vice President JD Vance on Monday downplayed the need for Americans to run out and buy emergency supplies – even as leaders in other parts of the world encouraged citizens to do so.
“A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water. My answer to that is no,” Vance told Fox News host Laura Ingraham.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
“We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything,” he said. “We want to make sure we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes.”
In the UK, meanwhile, officials recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, encouraging households to keep at least 72 hours’ worth of emergency supplies, food and water on-hand in case of a serious military threat.
In Japan, officials similarly launched an appeal to citizens urging them to maintain a week’s worth of water, perishable food and toilet supplies, according to the Times of Japan.
Costco did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

articles.title_zh: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
articles.content_orig:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII , launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.
The game has found more fans in recent months , but a portion of the Civilization audience will likely never fully warm to it due to its ages system—a design choice that partially solved many long-standing pacing problems, but at the cost of altering the core experience.
Before that, Firaxis worked on Marvel’s Midnight Suns , which had a more positive reception in terms of sentiment but does not seem to have sold as many units as the company had hoped. Now, with the new XCOM title facing challenges, that’s three troubled games in a row.
To top it off, most of Firaxis’ direct competitors in the strategy game market are much leaner and not beholden to a major publisher. (The publisher for the Civilization franchise is 2K Games, which lives under the same company that publishes the soon-to-launch Grand Theft Auto VI .)
The industry at large has seen widespread layoffs and studio closures over the past few years. There’s no single reason for that; rather, there are numerous factors, including contraction after COVID-era over-investment, increased competition, changes in leadership culture at major publishers, and larger economic factors beyond the scope of just the games industry.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title_orig: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
articles.title_zh: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services , for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS , Google Cloud Platform , and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products , Google Workspace , telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net . Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts .
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. articles.title_orig: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
articles.title_zh: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
articles.content_orig:
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400 . According to The Verge ’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.
While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today . That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.
Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.
On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK .

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.content_orig:
A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
“How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.
This story has been updated with additional content.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.title_zh: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.content_orig:
The US military has detained an American soldier accused of spying for Russia at a UK military base.
The senior officer, identified by The Telegraph as Lt Col Brandon Tyner, was first detained by UK counter-terrorism police in Gloucestershire on Nov 10.
On Tuesday, the 41-year-old was taken into custody by the US military over suspected national security and espionage allegations , according to the Metropolitan Police.
Asst Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of counter terrorism policing (CTP) in the UK, said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS, who in turn engaged with the Attorney General’s Office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.”
He added: “These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.”
He said UK police would “continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards”.
Kash Patel, the director of the FBI, said: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.”
Lt Col Tyner’s arrest followed a long-running investigation by British and American authorities, including MI5 and the FBI.
It is believed to be the first time a US soldier has been arrested on suspicion of spying offences on British soil.
Lt Col Tyner was assigned to Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He joined the US army in 2008 and served in Iraq, Afghanistan and Qatar, according to a US army official.
The Telegraph understands that he is suspected of sharing intelligence that would be highly damaging in the hands of a foreign power. However, officials are confident that no intelligence left the base.
It is believed that the soldier volunteered his services to Moscow, but was allegedly ensnared by undercover officers posing as Russian operatives.
Officials said his alleged motive was not clear.
He was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, the headquarters of the Nato Allied Rapid Reaction Corps and the UK’s largest Nato base.
Commanded by the British Army, the site hosts service members from more than 20 alliance nations. It holds a readiness force capable of deploying tens of thousands of troops on short notice and recently participated in an exercise modelling the defence of Europe.
An army official said Lt Col Tyner was expected to be prosecuted under the US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commander general of the US military’s counter-intelligence command, said: “This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution.”
Lt Col Tyner enlisted as a senior human resources officer in January 2008, a military official told The Telegraph.
He earned a bronze star for overseas deployment, having served in Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017 and Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014.
He was promoted to the rank of major in 2018 and lieutenant colonel in 2024.
The serviceman has regularly posted about cryptocurrency online. He also states on his social media that he volunteered at Burning Man festival, and describes himself as a “change agent”.
In his LinkedIn profile, Lt Col Tyner describes himself as a “disruptor” who “thrive[s] in high energy, ever evolving organisations with passions for diversity, growth, and cultural fitness”.

articles.title_orig: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.title_zh: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
As Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) prepares to begin trading under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19, business leaders are weighing in on the historically large initial public offering (IPO).
"There's no difference in investing in Anthropic on the IPO than Amazon on its IPO," "Shark Tank" host and O'Leary Ventures chair Kevin O'Leary said on Sozzi Unleashed . "There was tremendous volatility. It made zero money. But look at the platform it ultimately built. That's what you're betting on in the Anthropic deal."
Sitting down with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, O'Leary said the past few years haven't been great for buying IPOs, but he believes Anthropic may be a unique way to bet on artificial intelligence.
Anthropic said it expects to sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each. That would give the company a market valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion — putting it near SpaceX's ( SPCX ) IPO valuation of $1.77 trillion, which was the largest ever.
Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
"It may be the most hyped IPO ever," O'Leary said. "This IPO is the anchor to the entire AI or SI trade, whatever you want to call it."
What about the fact that Anthropic may not turn a profit until 2030? Though Anthropic's operating losses have improved, they still total $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year. The company also noted in its amended IPO filing that it plans to spend nearly $900 billion on computing and data centers, with $70 billion of that total coming due within a year.
O'Leary said Anthropic's profitability is the wrong lens right now. Buying in is a bet on AI's role across all 11 sectors of the economy, and he sees evidence of productivity and margin gains so far. That has helped markets remain near all-time highs despite tariffs, wars, and high energy prices.
These remarks follow O'Leary's comments last month, when the businessman called Anthropic "a hot trade."
"I expect it to be liquid from day one, and that changes the opportunity," he wrote in October.

articles.title_orig: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.title_zh: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill.
The funding request was suddenly increased from $30 billion after the hourslong ground stop Friday caused delays and cancellations for passengers across thousands of flights.
The formal funding ask was conveyed in a Tuesday letter signed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the failure, blaming it on predecessors and Congress. The letter, cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.”
After publicly reproaching Congress for the failure last week, Duffy met privately with Senate Republicans on Tuesday to make his case on Capitol Hill.
The closed-door briefing was contentious. The transportation secretary was “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators during his briefing, according to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion.
When it was over, Senate Republican leaders and Duffy notably held their news conferences separately.
Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stopped short of endorsing the full funding figure, saying only that the GOP is unified around the belief that “safe skies is an incredibly important priority.”
“We will see what the traffic will bear, what’s achievable,” he said, calling it a “discussion to be had” on the dollar amount.
Duffy met with only Republicans on Tuesday, not Democrats — even though the regular government funding process requires bipartisan support.
And Democrats were left wanting a better explanation, particularly as Duffy has pointed fingers at them. And members in both parties noted that President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up.
“Look, we have not been given the answers. They have not come clean,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Tuesday. “At his first press conference, all Duffy did was attack Democrats, and he asked for $50 billion when they haven’t even spent the $12 billion we’ve given to them. I have little faith in them.”
Facing Republican questions on the matter, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation.
Other Democrats are vexed by the FAA funding request.
“I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
The issue is wrapped up in a larger debate about funding the government ahead of a Dec. 11 deadline to avoid another shutdown . Congress could either reach a deal by then on new funding, punt it to next year with a stopgap bill, or fail to act and allow a shutdown.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said air traffic control is “absolutely not a partisan issue” and that Congress will work to make sure that any funding is “paid for in a responsible way.”
Republicans are also considering a party-line “reconciliation” bill to approve military funding without the need for Democratic votes; Democrats are likely to resist additional military funds unless the Iran war comes to an end. Other provisions could be added to such a bill — if it materializes before Republicans lose control of Congress. Thune indicated Tuesday that it is still an open question, as Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution by Thanksgiving to pull it off. It would be a long, arduous process requiring near-total GOP unity in both chambers, and it would need to begin soon in order to finish this year.
Duffy said he’s agnostic on how the funds get passed when asked by NBC News why he only met with Republicans on Tuesday.
“I have met with Democrats. I’ve spent hours on the phone with Democrats. Get along with them well. They understand this issue,” Duffy said Tuesday, speaking to reporters separately after meeting with GOP senators. “I’m not going to tell them how to do their work, but I’m telling everybody what we need. I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them work their process.”
One of the Democrats whom Duffy spoke to was House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely next House speaker.
“I appreciated the conversation,” Jeffries told reporters. “There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again.”
Jeffries added that he wants a briefing on the FAA ground stop and other recent outages, saying: “These developments are troubling, and it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure-related or whether there’s some malignant activity.”
When asked about Duffy’s $50.1 billion request, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Republicans would work with the administration to fund “as much of that as we can.” He pointed to the $12.5 billion already approved for FAA modernization and did not specify a timeline or whether Congress would pursue a supplemental funding package.
I am a field producer for NBC News based in Washington, D.C., covering all things politics.

articles.title_orig: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free
articles.title_zh: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free
articles.content_orig:
WhatsApp Android Apps Online services Social networks
WhatsApp started testing its encrypted cloud storage backup solution on Android in April and expanded testing to iOS in July. WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is now letting some beta users on Android back up their chats to its own encrypted cloud storage.
WABetaInfo found this in beta version 2.26.46.4 of WhatsApp for Android. It lets some beta users choose WhatsApp's cloud storage or Google Drive for backups.
WhatsApp offers 2GB of free cloud storage, but users can buy more through a WhatsApp Plus subscription, which provides 100GB of storage space. Those who want even more space can get up to 4TB of storage through Meta One. WhatsApp will automatically delete the backup permanently after four months if a user doesn't renew the subscription.
Note that chats backed up to WhatsApp's cloud storage are end-to-end encrypted by default, whereas those backed up to Google Drive (on Android) or iCloud (on iOS) aren't, since encryption is optional for those. If you don't want your chats encrypted for some reason, you'll have to switch back to Google Drive/iCloud, as encryption is mandatory for all data stored on WhatsApp's cloud storage.
WhatsApp users can also secure their backup on WhatsApp's cloud storage with a passkey , a password, or a 64-digit encryption key.
Since WhatsApp is already letting some beta users on Android back up their chats to its own cloud storage, we expect this feature to expand to beta users on iOS soon, followed by a public rollout for all users.

It's not for you, it's for WhatsApp and their third party vendors.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.title_zh: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.content_orig:
Firaxis, a sibling studio to Take-Two's Rockstar Games, is known for games like Sid Meier's Civilization VII and Marvel's Midnight Suns.
Take-Two Interactive is laying off employees at Firaxis Games, developer of Sid Meier's Civilization, Marvel's Midnight Suns , and the XCOM series. These layoffs at the Hunt Valley, MD-based studio come right before Take-Two's launch of Grand Theft Auto VI from subsidiary studio Rockstar Games and days after T2 shared its Q2 financial results .
A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two subsidiary that houses Firaxis, confirmed the layoffs in a statement to GameDeveloper.com. "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," they said.
"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology, and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."
Related: 'It's common for there to be speculation and headlines:' Unity exec addresses acquisition rumors
The spokesperson also disclosed that Firaxis head Heather Hazen is leaving the company. "With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start. "
"This is a hard day, but it’s a necessary one for the health and future of our studio, our game franchises and our fans who deserve the very best. We are deeply grateful for the contributions every member of the team has made."
Senior Editor, GameDeveloper.com

articles.title_orig: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
Some of the incidents reportedly involve Waymos in active construction zones.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after video showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told our sister station in the Bay Area.
SEE ALSO: California passenger stuck inside self-driving Waymo car through construction zone, followed by police
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026, Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says the new restrictions went into effect on Nov. 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. KGO-TV, our sister station in the Bay Area, previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again on Monday.
"I used to use it all the time, and now it's like, eh, I'll walk or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.title_zh: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.content_orig:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.
On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues .
Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.
So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com),  Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.
By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.

articles.title_zh: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
articles.content_orig:

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).
That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.
"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .
The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.
The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.
On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)
That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked.
"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.
Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.
Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.
If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .)
NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.
Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.
There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.
The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.
The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title_orig: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.title_zh: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it was experiencing tech issues Tuesday that were affecting several of its popular consumer-facing services.
As of 2 p.m. ET, Apple’s own system status page showed that Apple Business, Apple School Manager, AppleCare, iCloud Mail and Web Apps, and SchoolWork were each experiencing outages.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Earlier, the page showed the App Store and Apple Music experiencied outages.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” an Apple spokesperson told NBC News. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
At Apple stores in New York and Chicago, employees told NBC News earlier in the day that their internal software had stopped working and they had been unable to complete purchases or make appointments.
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Associated Press.
Gmail also appeared to experience an outage briefly Tuesday, with some users reporting issues accessing their email, according to Downdetector. The issue did not appear to be widespread and the company posted on X that they weren't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption."
The outages come on the heels of a string of major disruptions impacting U.S. services over the past several days — including Monday's Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo banking disruptions and United Airlines departing-flight system glitch , following Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop and Thursday's Microsoft cloud outage.
President Donald Trump brushed off the recent outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.”
“It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during his trip to the Philippines when asked about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
While none of the issues appear to be related, they’ve exposed America’s reliance on older infrastructure and revealed the extent to which companies and governments are being forced to upgrade systems in the AI age. The incidents have also stoked unfounded paranoia that something larger may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.title_zh: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts on Monday.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug,” a spokesperson said Monday. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
The Chase spokesperson went on to say it was a “bug,” rather than a widespread cyberattack.
Social media users reported issues with transactions at physical Chase branches, as well, and some local bank branches told customers earlier in the day that they were having issues with their internal system. However, Chase said in a statement that “customers still have access to their accounts and funds.”
The outage wasn’t caused by a cloud-related issue or a cyber attack, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. Rather, an update on the company’s own physical computer systems inadvertently caused issues.
As of 2:00 p.m. ET, more than 4,700 customers reported issues with Chase, according to Downdetector.
Customers reported issues at other major banks, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, though on a smaller scale.
The reports with the other banks appear to be related to sending money through Zelle, a digital payment network, to Chase accounts.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Bank of America also said it was operating normally on Monday.
“Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information,” a spokesperson told CNN.
Zelle said that its service is “operating as it should.” The money-transferring service is owned by a consortium of US banks called Early Warning Services, and Zelle said it does not hold consumer funds.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
Chase also said it wasn’t a systemic issue.
“Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” the spokesperson continued.
Monday’s Chase outage marked the third straight weekday with a massive technical failure.
On Thursday, a Microsoft outage cut off email access to millions of people across 74 countries and territories. On Friday, a Federal Aviation Administration systems failure led to a nationwide ground stop .
And on Monday afternoon, United Airlines reported a systemwide computer problem that delayed flights.
The incidents don’t share the same scope or root causes. Microsoft blamed a Windows defect, a traffic overload and capacity constraints. The FAA cited a router deployment issue and excessive data flooding its systems. It’s not yet clear what caused the Chase or United outages on Monday.
But the glitches share a common theme: “the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day,” Mike Chapple, a professor of IT, Analytics, and Operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in emailed comments.
“In each of these cases, what started as an issue in one small part of a larger system quickly spread, causing massive disruptions nationwide,” he added.
Complexity and interdependence aren’t inherently flaws — in fact, they make systems more resilient, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.
“But when dependencies on systems aren’t sufficiently understood, failures can cascade across institutions and industries,” she added.
Think about it like the Titanic: The watertight bulkheads were unable to withstand a failure that exceeded the ship’s architects’ worst-case-scenario assumptions. Even the best-designed systems sometimes succumb to threats and problems that the designers couldn’t have imagined when they built them.
The problem with interdependent technology systems is that system failures are rarely isolated incidents: Our heavy reliance on a handful of systems means failures have tended to bring down systems across the world.
“The question for leaders is not whether one system will fail but how many other things fail with it, and how fast you can contain it,” said Madhu Shashanka, founder of Concentric AI.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.title_zh: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.content_orig:
Apple said an internal update was to blame for a major outage on Nov. 17 that hit its App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay and other software, with thousands of users reporting problems online.
In a statement to USA TODAY, Apple said it was working to fix the affected systems, and services are expected to return to normal soon.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," the company said.
Apple, on its System Status page , confirmed outages on App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, as well as issues with iCloud Account & Sign In. The company told Bloomberg the problems weren't caused by a cyberattack.
According to outage tracker Downdetector, reports of issues with Apple Pay began to spike at around 11:40 a.m. ET with a peak of reports at around 12:15 p.m. ET. Outage reports for iCloud also started to surge just before noon ET, though reports on Downdetector don't reflect every user experiencing a problem. Those reports had dropped significantly by mid-afternoon.
The Apple software issues came on the heels of a major banking outage on Nov. 16 that stemmed from Chase Bank. It also impacted Wells Fargo, Bank of America, online payment platform Zelle and other institutions.
Last week, a communications outage disrupted air traffic across the United States, and a Microsoft outage prevented many from checking their Outlook email and accessing Microsoft 365 services like Teams and Word.

articles.title_zh: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.content_orig:
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ASSOCIATED PRESS
Published: 17:12 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 08:04 EST, 17 November 2026
United Airlines flights across the United States were grounded on Monday night, just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground all flights nationwide.
The airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'
'We're aware of the widespread system and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible,' it posted on X.
'We appreciate your patience while we work through this,' the airline added, urging anyone with scheduled flights to keep checking their flight status on the app.
The post has since been deleted, as a spokesperson for the airline told the Daily Mail that the issue has been resolved.
'While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the spokesperson said, adding: 'There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.'
The update came after frustrated travelers took to social media to bemoan how their flights could not take off.
'Currently stuck on the tarmac,' one X user posted, blaming it on an IT issue in which the airline 'can't clear planes for takeoff as [they] can't connect to the weight system.'
United Airlines flights across the country were grounded Monday night as the airline experienced a 'widespread system outage'
The issue comes just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to ground all flights nationwide
United Airlines said on social media its teams were 'working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible'
The outage is now the latest in a string of technical issues that have crippled businesses around the country and left airline passengers stranded for hours amid a rare nationwide ground stop.
Earlier Monday, thousands of customers with Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo also flagged being unable to log in or transfer money , according to Down Detector, a website which tracks real-time user reports.
A spokesperson for Chase told the Daily Mail the outage was caused by a technical bug.
'Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,' they said. 'We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.'
Chase also addressed one complaint on X, telling a client: 'I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking.
'Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience.'
Wells Fargo also posted a note on its website telling customers that 'online banking isn't available right now' due to 'technical issues'.
A spokesperson for Chase later noted that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related,' said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
'This is not a systemic issue - other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,' he said.
Customers at three major US banks have been locked out of their accounts as Chase and Wells Fargo all experienced outages on Monday afternoon
Over 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that 'clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.'
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
'An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,' the spokesman said.
Still, the outage sparked panic as it came just three days after Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday , leaving people unable to access Outlook, Teams and Copilot applications.
Businesses ground to a halt, healthcare providers lost contact with patients, courts lost live feeds, and governments struggled to communicate.
The suspected cause was a faulty network configuration change that resulted in numerous servers becoming unavailable, overloading the remaining infrastructure.
The FAA also issued a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following a major communications failure on Friday.
'What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' Trump said on Monday of the FAA outage that forced thousands of cancelled and delayed flights over the weekend
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) said on Friday that the  halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'.
'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said.
'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'
President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers.
'We have old, broken equipment,' the President said Monday at the White House before departing for his trip to Asia on board the new Air Force One plane gifted to the administration by Qatari officials.
He noted that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.
'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
The incident marked only the second time since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that a nationwide ground stop was implemented.
The stoppage also prevented any domestic flights from taking off, resulting in one of the worst travel snarls in recent US history. It began around 3.30pm and was not lifted until around 8.20pm.
More than 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday.
It is estimated that more than one million American travelers have been impacted by the outage.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy claimed Biden-era upgrades were shoddy
The President also cast blame on his predecessor for the FAA glitch.
'The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass. So a lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old,' Trump said.
He was referring to Biden-era upgrades to communication systems built on copper wiring that were upgraded to fiber-optic, or glass, wires.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the upgrade work was shoddy, resulting in the outage.
Trump said the upgrade was a waste of money and more cash would be needed from Congress to fully upgrade the system and prevent future issues.
'We want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress,' the President told reporters.
